issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not interfere with a High Court acquittal in an appeal under Article 136 unless the High Court’s appraisal of the evidence is affected by a glaring infirmity; the possibility of another view is insufficient.
material_facts: The State appealed by special leave against the High Court’s acquittal of the accused.
The trial court’s convictions rested on the eyewitness testimony of one witness.
The High Court found that witness’s testimony unreliable because of inconsistencies, possible influence, and the possible false implication of several people.
The Supreme Court found no glaring infirmity in the High Court’s appraisal of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the acquittal and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not interfere with a High Court finding of acquittal unless the finding is vitiated by a glaring infirmity in the appraisal of evidence. The fact that another view of the evidence could have been taken does not justify interference. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a High Court acquittal.
predicates.high_court_appraisal_not_glaringly_defec: The Supreme Court finds no glaring defect in the High Court’s assessment of the evidence.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and the High Court’s evidence appraisal has no glaring defect, the acquittal remains undisturbed.
